original_question: Let lambda_n(s) be the canonically indexed eigenvalues of the Mayer-Ruelle transfer operator for the Gauss continued-fraction map, indexed so that the labeling by n is canonical and corresponds to ordering by magnitude. For each nontrivial zero rho of the Riemann zeta function, let t(rho) be the integer M such that lambda_M(rho/2) = 1. Given a fixed integer M in N, determine what can be said about the set t^(-1)(M): whether it is infinite, how the conjectural distribution of Riemann zeros changes when restricted to that set, and how one can compute sets such as t^(-1)(1) effectively.
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 4: "Map from set of non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function to the set of eigenvalues of the transfer operator for the Gauss continued fraction map."
correct_elements: Your draft already tracks Section 3, Problem 4 very closely. It correctly focuses on the Mayer-Ruelle transfer operator for the Gauss continued-fraction map, the canonically indexed eigenvalues lambda_n(s), the condition lambda_M(rho/2) = 1 for nontrivial zeta zeros rho, and the three questions the paper actually asks: whether the fiber t^(-1)(M) is infinite, how the distribution of Riemann zeros changes on that restricted fiber, and how to compute a concrete fiber effectively. It also correctly uses the +1 condition, which is the sign singled out in the paper for Riemann zeros and even Maass wave forms.
missing_details: The paper first fixes the analytic setting: D is the disc { z in C : |z - 1| < 3/2 }, and B(D) is the Banach space of functions analytic on D and continuous on its closure, with the supremum norm.

To make the question stand-alone, the Mayer-Ruelle operator itself should be stated explicitly: for Re(s) > 1/2, (L_s f)(z) = sum_{n >= 1} (z+n)^(-2s) f(1/(z+n)), with analytic continuation in s to all complex values.

The paper motivates lambda_M(rho/2) = 1 via Mayer's determinant identity relating the Fredholm determinant of L_s to the Selberg zeta function for the full modular group; that context should be mentioned so the condition does not look ad hoc.

The canonical indexing is not just 'by magnitude': in the paper's surrounding discussion it is tied to the indexing by polynomial degree n, and the paper stresses that this canonical attribution of the index is crucial.

If the notation t(rho) is retained, its well-definedness should be stated carefully; a cleaner stand-alone formulation is to avoid the map notation and work directly with the fiber set { rho : lambda_M(rho/2) = 1 }.
The paper explicitly distinguishes the relevant +1 condition from the -1 condition: +1 corresponds to Riemann zeros and even Maass wave forms, whereas -1 corresponds to odd Maass wave forms.
The quantifier on M should be stated explicitly as 'for a fixed positive integer M'.
If one keeps the effective-computation clause, the concrete sample fiber should be defined explicitly as S_1 = { rho : lambda_1(rho/2) = 1 } rather than left implicit.
refined_question: Let D = { z in C : |z - 1| < 3/2 }, let B(D) be the Banach space of functions analytic on D and continuous on its closure with the supremum norm, and for Re(s) > 1/2 let L_s be the Mayer-Ruelle transfer operator for the Gauss continued-fraction map, defined by (L_s f)(z) = sum_{n >= 1} (z+n)^(-2s) f(1/(z+n)), analytically continued in s to all complex values. Write lambda_n(s) for the canonically indexed eigenvalues of L_s, where the canonical index is the one described in the paper (equivalently, the index attached via polynomial degree and hence by ordering according to magnitude). Using Mayer's determinant relation with the Selberg zeta function, and restricting to the relevant +1/even factor, define for each fixed M in N the fiber S_M = { rho : rho is a nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function and lambda_M(rho/2) = 1 }. For a fixed M, what can be said about S_M: is it infinite, how should the conjectural distribution of Riemann zeros change when restricted to S_M, and how can one effectively compute concrete fibers such as S_1?
justification: The nearest official target is plainly Problem 4 in Section 3, not a broader neighboring problem. Your draft is already almost a paraphrase of that problem. The only real work needed is to supply the operator/Banach-space setup from the paragraph immediately preceding Problem 4, make the canonical indexing assumption explicit in the same way the paper does, and preserve the paper's sign convention (+1, not -1). I therefore kept the scope exactly fiberwise in M and did not broaden it into a general study of the whole spectrum or of all Selberg-zeta zeros. I also avoided introducing a stronger formal map t unless its fiber is explicitly defined, because the paper's point is really the study of the sets cut out by lambda_M(rho/2) = 1.
